claim: In plants, clathrin mediated endocytosis (CME) represents the major route for cargo internalisation from the cell surface.
source: In plants, clathrin mediated endocytosis (CME) represents the major route for cargo internalisation from the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational claim about plant CME.

claim: Arabidopsis CME follows the constant curvature model.
source: Arabidopsis CME appears to follow the constant curvature model and the bona fide CME population generates vesicles of a predominantly hexagonal-basket type
evidence: This claim is supported by ultrastructural analysis using SEM and live imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The bona fide CME population in Arabidopsis generates vesicles of a predominantly hexagonal-basket type.
source: Arabidopsis CME appears to follow the constant curvature model and the bona fide CME population generates vesicles of a predominantly hexagonal-basket type
evidence: This is supported by SEM analysis of clathrin-coated structures showing hexagonal basket predominance.

claim: Arabidopsis CME vesicles are larger than in other models.
source: Arabidopsis CME appears to follow the constant curvature model and the bona fide CME population generates vesicles of a predominantly hexagonal-basket type; larger and with faster kinetics than in other models.
evidence: This is supported by comparative measurements of vesicle sizes between Arabidopsis and other model systems.

claim: Arabidopsis CME has faster kinetics than in other models.
source: Arabidopsis CME appears to follow the constant curvature model and the bona fide CME population generates vesicles of a predominantly hexagonal-basket type; larger and with faster kinetics than in other models.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF-M measurements showing CME lifetimes of 33-42 seconds compared to longer times in yeast.

claim: Actin is dispensable for CME events at the plasma membrane in plants.
source: Contrary to the existing paradigm, actin is dispensable for CME events at the plasma membrane but plays a unique role in collecting endocytic vesicles, sorting of internalised cargos and directional endosome movement that itself actively promote CME events.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that actin perturbation does not affect CME kinetics or efficiency at the PM.

claim: Actin plays a unique role in collecting endocytic vesicles in plants.
source: Contrary to the existing paradigm, actin is dispensable for CME events at the plasma membrane but plays a unique role in collecting endocytic vesicles, sorting of internalised cargos and directional endosome movement that itself actively promote CME events.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging showing endosomes picking up CCVs and ultrastructural evidence of CCVs on actin filaments.

claim: Actin plays a role in sorting of internalised cargos in plants.
source: Contrary to the existing paradigm, actin is dispensable for CME events at the plasma membrane but plays a unique role in collecting endocytic vesicles, sorting of internalised cargos and directional endosome movement that itself actively promote CME events.
evidence: This is supported by observations of PIN2 mislocalization after actin perturbation.

claim: Actin-mediated directional endosome movement actively promotes CME events in plants.
source: Contrary to the existing paradigm, actin is dispensable for CME events at the plasma membrane but plays a unique role in collecting endocytic vesicles, sorting of internalised cargos and directional endosome movement that itself actively promote CME events.
evidence: This is supported by the endosomal pick-up analysis showing increased CME termination when endosomes pass by.

claim: Internalized vesicles in plants display a strongly delayed and sequential uncoating.
source: Internalized vesicles display a strongly delayed and sequential uncoating.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging showing CCVs retaining clathrin coat until reaching endosomes and sequential loss of coat components.

claim: Plant CME mechanism evolved independently during the autonomous rise of multicellularity in eukaryotes.
source: These unique features highlight the independent evolution of the plant CME mechanism during the autonomous rise of multicellularity in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the multiple unique features of plant CME compared to other eukaryotic models.

claim: CME is the key cellular process of internalising cargo from the plasma membrane or outside the cell.
source: Clathrin mediated endocytosis (CME) is the key cellular progress of internalising a cargo, either on the plasma membrane (PM) or outside the cell, into the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CME function.

claim: CME cargos are packaged inside vesicles covered by a coat made of the protein clathrin.
source: The cargos are packaged inside a small vesicle, which is covered by a coat made of the protein clathrin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CME mechanism.

claim: CME represents a major endocytic route in eukaryotes.
source: CME represents a major endocytic route in eukaryotes (Goh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Most, if not all, endocytosis in plants occurs via CME.
source: In plants, it is even more significant as most, if not all, endocytosis occurs via CME
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with some uncertainty ('if not all').

claim: Many important PM proteins implicated in key physiological processes are established cargos for the CME pathway in plants.
source: many important PM proteins implicated in key physiological processes, such as growth and development, nutrient uptake or pathogen defence, are established cargos for the CME pathway (Barberon et al., 2011; Dhonukshe et al., 2007; Di Rubbo et al., 2013; Mbengue et al., 2016; Yoshinari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: CME in plants represents a major mechanism for regulating both local cellular signaling and the global response to external stimuli.
source: Therefore, CME in plants represents a major mechanism for regulating both local cellular signaling and the global response to external stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the importance of CME cargos in various physiological processes.

claim: CME in plants is poorly characterized.
source: CME in plants is poorly characterized and its hypothesized mechanism is largely inferred from studies in mammalian and yeast systems
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study.

claim: The hypothesized mechanism of plant CME is largely inferred from studies in mammalian and yeast systems.
source: CME in plants is poorly characterized and its hypothesized mechanism is largely inferred from studies in mammalian and yeast systems, where CME components are highly conserved
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the state of the field.

claim: CME components are highly conserved between mammalian and yeast systems.
source: CME in plants is poorly characterized and its hypothesized mechanism is largely inferred from studies in mammalian and yeast systems, where CME components are highly conserved; with at least 60 homologous endocytosis accessory proteins (EAPs) well characterized in both these model systems (Kaksonen and Roux, 2018; Lu et al., 2016; Merrifield and Kaksonen, 2014; Taylor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At least 60 homologous endocytosis accessory proteins (EAPs) are well characterized in both mammalian and yeast systems.
source: CME in plants is poorly characterized and its hypothesized mechanism is largely inferred from studies in mammalian and yeast systems, where CME components are highly conserved; with at least 60 homologous endocytosis accessory proteins (EAPs) well characterized in both these model systems (Kaksonen and Roux, 2018; Lu et al., 2016; Merrifield and Kaksonen, 2014; Taylor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Plants possess homologues of many of the core EAPs.
source: Plants possess homologues of the many of the core EAPs
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about plant CME components.

claim: There are two clathrin heavy chain proteins (CHC 1 and 2) in plants.
source: for example, there are two clathrin heavy chain proteins (CHC 1 and 2) and three clathrin light chains (CLC 1, 2 and 3, which have at least 30% sequence homology with mammalian CLCa and CLCb Wang et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: There are three clathrin light chains (CLC 1, 2 and 3) in plants.
source: for example, there are two clathrin heavy chain proteins (CHC 1 and 2) and three clathrin light chains (CLC 1, 2 and 3, which have at least 30% sequence homology with mammalian CLCa and CLCb Wang et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Plant clathrin light chains have at least 30% sequence homology with mammalian CLCa and CLCb.
source: for example, there are two clathrin heavy chain proteins (CHC 1 and 2) and three clathrin light chains (CLC 1, 2 and 3, which have at least 30% sequence homology with mammalian CLCa and CLCb Wang et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Functional characterisation of plant EAPs is greatly lacking.
source: However, functional characterisation of these, and other plant EAPs, is greatly lacking.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge motivating the study.

claim: There are key differences in the actual CME mechanism between mammalian and yeast systems, chiefly related to the requirement of actin cytoskeleton.
source: Despite a high degree of conservation between mammalian and yeast EAPs, there are key differences in the actual CME mechanism; chiefly related to the requirement of actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about differences between model systems.

claim: Actin co-localises with single sites of CME in both mammalian and yeast systems.
source: While actin co-localises with single sites of CME in both systems, interference with actin results in a total arrest of CME in yeast (Kaksonen et al., 2005) whereas in mammalian cells, there is only an overall reduction of endocytosis but still ongoing productive CME events (Fujimoto et al., 2000; Merrifield et al., 2005; Taylor et al., 2012; Yarar et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Interference with actin results in a total arrest of CME in yeast.
source: While actin co-localises with single sites of CME in both systems, interference with actin results in a total arrest of CME in yeast (Kaksonen et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In mammalian cells, actin interference causes only an overall reduction of endocytosis but still ongoing productive CME events.
source: whereas in mammalian cells, there is only an overall reduction of endocytosis but still ongoing productive CME events (Fujimoto et al., 2000; Merrifield et al., 2005; Taylor et al., 2012; Yarar et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The difference in actin requirement between yeast and mammalian CME has been attributed to the higher turgor pressure of cell wall-encapsulated yeast cells.
source: This difference has been attributed to the higher turgor pressure of the cell wall-encapsulated yeast cells (Aghamohammadzadeh and Ayscough, 2009; Boulant et al., 2011; Dmitrieff and Nédélec, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Plant cells are subject to equal or even higher turgor pressures compared to yeast cells.
source: As plant cells are subject to equal or even higher turgor pressures compared to yeast cells (Beauzamy et al., 2014; Schaber et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Actin has been hypothesized to be crucial for plant CME.
source: As plant cells are subject to equal or even higher turgor pressures compared to yeast cells (Beauzamy et al., 2014; Schaber et al., 2010), actin has been hypothesized to be crucial for plant CME
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on turgor pressure considerations.

claim: The role of actin in plant CME has not been assessed in great detail.
source: actin has been hypothesized to be crucial for plant CME; nonetheless, it has not been assessed in great detail.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: One major reason for lack of knowledge about plant CME is the inability to directly observe CME and clathrin coated vesicles (CCVs) in vivo.
source: One of the major reasons for this is the inability to directly observe CME and clathrin coated vesicles (CCVs) in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation in the field.

claim: Electron microscopy was the key technology credited for the first CME characterisation.
source: For example, electron microscopy, the key technology credited for the first CME characterisation (Roth and Porter, 1964; Schmid et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Electron microscopy can be performed with plant tissues.
source: For example, electron microscopy, the key technology credited for the first CME characterisation (Roth and Porter, 1964; Schmid et al., 2014), can be performed with plant tissues (Robinson, 1996; Valk and Fowke, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Successful capturing of ongoing CME events in plant tissues using electron microscopy is rare.
source: can be performed with plant tissues (Robinson, 1996; Valk and Fowke, 2011) but the successful capturing of ongoing CME events is rare.
evidence: This is stated as a technical challenge in the field.

claim: The plant field has recently started to adopt live imaging methods to directly look at the dynamics of CME events.
source: It is only recently that the plant field has started to adopt live imaging methods to directly look at the dynamics of CME events; like total internal reflective microscopy (TIRF-M) (Johnson and Vert, 2017; Vizcay-Barrena et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Metal replicas of Arabidopsis root protoplast cells provided a detailed view of well-preserved CCPs at various stages of invagination at the PM.
source: Metal replicas of Arabidopsis root protoplast cells provided a detailed view of well-preserved CCPs at various stages of invagination at the PM and fully formed CCVs deeper inside the cell, which are often attached to cytoskeletal and intracellular membrane structures (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by SEM images shown in the figures.

claim: Metal replicas of Arabidopsis root protoplast cells showed fully formed CCVs deeper inside the cell, which are often attached to cytoskeletal and intracellular membrane structures.
source: Metal replicas of Arabidopsis root protoplast cells provided a detailed view of well-preserved CCPs at various stages of invagination at the PM and fully formed CCVs deeper inside the cell, which are often attached to cytoskeletal and intracellular membrane structures (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by SEM images shown in the figures.

claim: Resin embedded sections technique was less efficient than metal replica for observing CCSs.
source: However, this technique was less efficient than metal replica, as we could observe only a few CCSs and we could not obtain tomographic reconstuctions to detemine the composition of clathrin polygons which make up the whole coat (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of results from the two techniques.

claim: The hexagonal basket population has diameter ranging from 46 to 81 nm with a mean of 66.1 nm.
source: The hexagonal basket population has diameter, ranging from 46 to 81 nm with a mean of 66.1 nm.
evidence: This is based on measurements from SEM images.

claim: The diameter of pentagonal basket population ranges from 41 to 72 with a mean of 59.9 nm.
source: The diameter of pentagonal basket population range from 41 to 72 with a mean of 59.9 nm (15 cells, 188 CCSs measured).
evidence: This is based on measurements from SEM images.

claim: The diameter for the irregularly ordered baskets ranged between 62–113 nm with a mean of 85 nm.
source: The diameter for the irregularly ordered baskets ranged between 62–113 nm with a mean of 85 nm (15 cells, 72 CCSs measured)
evidence: This is based on measurements from SEM images.

claim: Differences in CCS sizes could be due to differences in the numbers of hexagonal clathrin rings.
source: A possible reason for the differences in sizes could be due differences in the numbers of hexagonal clathrin rings, as CCVs are expected to contain 12 pentagons and a different number of hexagons alters the overall size (den Otter and Briels, 2011; Cheng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The frequency distribution of CCS populations are similar in both the PM and the intracellular membrane, with the prominent type being hexagonal (60%).
source: We observed CCSs conforming to all typical basket types (Figure 1G), and the frequency distribution of the populations are similar in both the PM and the intracellular membrane; with the prominent type being hexagonal (60%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of CCS types from SEM images.

claim: Multiple CCSs fused together are typically found on intracellular membranes.
source: Typically for intracellular membranes there were multiple CCSs fused together, the occasional occurrence of huge CCSs and also large aggregations of CCSs comprising of same or different population types (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is based on observations from SEM images.

claim: Intracellular membrane structures with CCSs have been previously reported to be the early endosome/trans-Golgi network (EE/TGN) or the partially-coated reticulum.
source: These intracellular membrane structures have been previously reported to be the early endosome/trans-Golgi network (EE/TGN) or the partially-coated reticulum (Galway et al., 1993; Kang et al., 2011; Robinson, 2015; Tanchak et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CCSs at the intracellular membrane structures could be secretory vesicles budding off the TGN.
source: The CCSs at the intracellular membrane structures could be secretory vesicles budding off the TGN (Kirchhausen, 2000; Kural et al., 2012; Robinson and Pimpl, 2014; Watanabe et al., 2014)
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: If uncoating in plants is delayed, CCSs at intracellular membrane structures can be endocytosed CCVs fusing to the EE.
source: or if the uncoating in plants would be delayed, they can be also endocytosed CCVs fusing to the EE.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation.

claim: There was an absence of large clathrin assemblies or lattices in Arabidopsis.
source: First, we found that there was an absence of large clathrin assemblies or lattices in Arabidopsis (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on observations from SEM images.

claim: Most of the lattices found in Arabidopsis were small, with only a few clathrin polygons.
source: Most of the lattices that were found were small, with only a few clathrin polygons, consistent with early reports in other plant species (Coleman et al., 1988; Emons, 1986).
evidence: This is based on observations from SEM images and supported by citations.

claim: Less than 4% of the CCPs formed a flat structure.
source: We found that less than 4% of the CCPs formed a flat structure (Supplementary file 1 - table 1).
evidence: This is based on quantification of CCP structures from SEM images.

claim: 47 dome-shaped and 16 spherical CCPs exhibited the same en face view (hexagonal basket shape).
source: We then analyzed the en face surface-view of the dome-shaped and spherical CCPs and found that 47 of the dome-shaped and 16 of the spherical CCPs exhibited the same en face view; the hexagonal basket shape.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SEM images.

claim: Hexagonal basket-type CCPs at different stages of development possess a constant radius of curvature.
source: This result highlights that hexagonal basket-type CCPs at different stages of development possess a constant radius of curvature (Figure 1C and H and Supplementary file 1 - table 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of en face views from SEM images.

claim: Predominantly the CCPs constituting the hexagonal and pentagonal basket-type populations undergo membrane bending following the constant curvature model.
source: This demonstrates that predominantly the CCPs constituting the hexagonal and pentagonal basket-type populations undergo membrane bending following the constant curvature model.
evidence: This is based on analysis of CCP structures at different developmental stages.

claim: The diameters of the CCVs measured in unroofed protoplast cells is similar to CCVs purified from the entire seedlings.
source: Interestingly, the diameters of the CCVs measured in our unroofed protoplast cells is similar to CCVs purified from the entire seedlings (where the CCV size ranges between 60–80 nm [Mosesso et al., 2018; Reynolds et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous literature.

claim: It is very likely that both the protoplasts and intact plant systems have similar mechanisms of CCV formation.
source: Therefore, it is very likely that the both the protoplasts and intact plant systems have similar mechanisms of CCV formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on similarity of CCV sizes.

claim: TIRF-M detected small foci rather than large plaques of fluorescence signal in root epidermis expressing CLC2-GFP.
source: We directly observed the PMs of root epidermis expressing clathrin light chain two tagged with GFP (CLC2-GFP) and detected small foci rather than large plaques of fluorescence signal (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on TIRF-M imaging data.

claim: Large clathrin structures present in live tissue images are highly mobile and represent EE/TGN structures.
source: There are large clathrin structures present in the live tissue images, however they are highly mobile (Figure 4—video 2 – control condition, and Figure 5—video 3) and represent EE/TGN structures (Figure 1F), therefore they are not attached to the PM.
evidence: This is based on live imaging observations.

claim: The intensity profile of clathrin tracks shows an initial steep increase of signal, followed by a plateau phase, and finally a sharp drop in intensity.
source: The intensity profile show an initial steep increase of signal (representing the assembly of clathrin at the pit), followed by a plateau phase (representing the maturation phase of the CCP), and finally a sharp drop in intensity (corresponding to the scission and release of the CCV) (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is based on analysis of TIRF-M imaging data.

claim: The clathrin intensity profile is reminiscent of the clathrin intensity profiles reported in mammalian cells.
source: which is reminiscent of the clathrin intensity profiles reported in mammalian cells (Loerke et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: The maturation phase accounts for only 17.8 ± 8% of the entire span of CCP development.
source: The maturation phase accounts for only 17.8 ± 8% of the entire span of development, while the assembly phase takes up to 42 ± 5%.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of intensity profiles.

claim: The assembly phase takes up to 42 ± 5% of the entire span of CCP development.
source: The maturation phase accounts for only 17.8 ± 8% of the entire span of development, while the assembly phase takes up to 42 ± 5%.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of intensity profiles.

claim: The segregation in the intensity profile is suggestive of the 'constant curvature' rather than 'constant area' model.
source: Such segregation in the intensity profile is suggestive of the 'constant curvature', rather than 'constant area' model, which entails a short assembly and very long maturation phases (Avinoam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with expected profiles for different models.

claim: A large data set of lifetimes was generated by imaging plant root epidermis expressing CLC2-GFP (12 cells and 149162 tracks).
source: A large data set of lifetimes was generated (12 cells and 149162 tracks) by imaging plant root epidermis expressing CLC2-GFP.
evidence: This describes the experimental dataset.

claim: The mean lifetime of all the clathrin CLC2 tracks was 20 s.
source: The mean lifetime of all the clathrin CLC2 tracks was 20 s, which closely matches the lifetime reported based on manual measurements (Konopka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TIRF-M tracking data.

claim: Statistical testing revealed that three populations produced the best fit for clathrin lifetime data.
source: Further statistical testing of the experimental data revealed that three populations produced the best fit (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling of lifetime distributions.

claim: Two short-lived sub-populations were identified with lifetimes of 2 s (accounting for 6.31% of the total population) and 9 s (accounting for 50.6% of the total population).
source: There were two short-lived sub-populations identified with lifetimes of 2 s (accounting for 6.31% of the total population) and 9 s (accounting for 50.6% of the total population).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling of lifetime distributions.

claim: The third population accounts for 43.9% of all clathrin on the surface and had a lifetime of 42 s.
source: The third population accounts for 43.9% of all clathrin on the surface and had a lifetime of 42 s (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling of lifetime distributions.

claim: The mean lifetime of tracks positive for both CLC2 and TPLATE markers was 42 s.
source: One would expect bona fide CME events to be positive for both markers and indeed, the mean lifetime of the tracks positive for both markers was 42 s (Figure 2C,D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on dual-channel TIRF-M imaging data.

claim: The lifetime of CLC2 when colocalized with adaptor AP2 was found to be 43 s.
source: Additionally, the lifetime of CLC2 when colocalized with another adaptor AP2 (Di Rubbo et al., 2013) confirmed these observations, as its lifetime was found to be similar, 43 s.
evidence: This is based on dual-channel TIRF-M imaging data.

claim: The lifetime of CME events in root is about 42 s.
source: Thus, the empirically obtained bona fide population of endocytic events matches the mathematically simulated longer-lived sub-population collectively suggesting the lifetime of CME events in root to be about 42 s.
evidence: This is based on convergence of mathematical modeling and empirical measurements.

claim: The mean lifetime of bona fide CME events in Arabidopsis hypocotyl epidermis is 33 s.
source: The same analysis of CLC2 and TPLATE positive tracks in Arabidopsis hypocotyl epidermis produced a significantly shorter mean lifetime of 33 s (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is based on TIRF-M imaging data from hypocotyl tissue.

claim: There is organ-specific regulation of CME in plants.
source: Thus, the mathematical analysis of CLC2 lifetime histograms and dual channel TIRF-M imaging independently reveal a lifetime of about 42 and 33 s for the bona fide CME events in root and shoot cells, respectively and suggested a so far unappreciated organ-specific regulation of CME in plants.
evidence: This is an inference based on differences in CME lifetimes between organs.

claim: In yeast and mammalian cells with high membrane tension, actin is considered the major force generator aiding membrane invagination.
source: In yeast, and in mammalian cells with high membrane tension, actin is considered the major force generator aiding membrane invagination (Kaksonen and Roux, 2018; Kaksonen et al., 2005; Saleem et al., 2015; Stachowiak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Actin polymerizes around the endocytic pit and aids the invagination to form against the tension and turgor pressure.
source: Actin polymerizes around the endocytic pit and with pushing and pulling actions, it aids the invagination to form against the tension and turgor pressure (Brady et al., 2010; Buser and Drubin, 2013; Picco et al., 2015; Toshima et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Plant cells possess high turgor pressure values 0.3–1 MPa.
source: Plant cells, similar to yeast are enclosed within a cell wall and possess high turgor pressure values 0.3–1 MPa (Cosgrove, 1993)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Actin has been assumed to play a key role in membrane invagination during plant endocytosis.
source: therefore actin has been assumed to play a key role in membrane invagination during plant endocytosis (Chen et al., 2011; Robatzek et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Using SEM on unroofed protoplasts, actin exhibits a more complicated network deeper inside the cell.
source: Deeper inside the cell, actin exhibits a more complicated network (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is based on SEM observations.

claim: Closer to the PM, only thick main filaments and several thinner subsidiary filaments were observed, but never an enrichment of actin around the CCPs.
source: but closer to the PM, we observed only thick main filaments and several thinner subsidiary filaments but, unexpectedly, never an enrichment of actin around the CCPs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on SEM observations.

claim: No actin concentrations at the PM around the CCPs marked by CLC2-mKO were observed using TIRF-M.
source: In accordance with our SEM analysis of the protoplast replicas, we observed no actin concentrations at the PM around the CCPs marked by CLC2-mKusabira-Orange (mKO).
evidence: This is based on TIRF-M imaging data.

claim: In root hair cells, actin did not form concentrate foci on the PM, unlike the CCP markers.
source: In addition, in root hair cells, when we assessed the localization of actin and the localizations of CCPs at the PM (marked by Dynamin-Related Protein (Drp1C)), actin did not form concentrate foci on the PM, unlike the CCP markers (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy imaging data.

claim: After prolonged treatment with Jasp or LatB, CCVs marked by CLC2-mKO formed and were removed from the PM with no apparent arrest of pits.
source: After prolonged treatment with 10 µM Jasp that lead to extreme structural abnormalities of the actin filaments, or 10 uM LatB that lead to overall depolymerisation of the actin network, CCVs marked by CLC2-mKO formed and were removed from the PM with no apparent arrest of pits (Figure 3—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on TIRF-M imaging after drug treatments.

claim: No clear changes in the overall lifetime distribution and foci density of EAPs were observed after LatB and Jasp treatments.
source: Moreover, we observed no clear changes in the overall lifetime distribution and foci density of any of these EAPs after 10 µM LatB and 5 µM Jasp treatments in both hypocotyl and root epidermal cells (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 1 - table 2).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of TIRF-M data after drug treatments.

claim: No significant changes in the average duration of any of the developmental phases (CCP initiation, maturation or scission) were observed after LatB treatment.
source: Again, we saw no significant changes in the average duration of any of the developmental phases: CCP initiation, maturation or scission, after LatB treatment.
evidence: This is based on analysis of intensity profiles after drug treatment.

claim: After LatB and Jasp treatments, PM internalization of FM4-64 still occurred.
source: We used the endocytic tracer, the dye FM4-64 (Jelínková et al., 2010) in root cells and observed that after LatB and Jasp treatments, PM internalization still occurred (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy imaging after drug treatments.

claim: Following LatB treatment, FLS2 endocytosis still occurred and the receptors reached the endosomes.
source: Again, following LatB treatment, FLS2 endocytosis still occurred and the receptors reached the endosomes, as expected (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is based on TIRF-M imaging after drug treatment.

claim: Overexpressing AUXILIN-LIKE2 reduced the PIN2 endocytic rate.
source: To validate this assay, we examined the PIN2-Dendra endocytic rate by overexpressing AUXILIN-LIKE2, which has been shown to inhibit CME (Adamowski et al., 2018), and found that the PIN2 endocytic rate was reduced (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is based on photoconversion experiments.

claim: LatB treatment led to no significant change in the PIN2 endocytic uptake.
source: In contrast, LatB treatment led to no significant change in the PIN2 endocytic uptake (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is based on photoconversion experiments after drug treatment.

claim: Acute and chronic perturbations of the actin network do not have a major impact on CCP formation, CME dynamics or CME of multiple cargos in both Arabidopsis roots and hypocotyls.
source: In conclusion, these multiple quantitative observations show that acute as well as chronic perturbations of the actin network do not have a major impact on CCP formation, CME dynamics or CME of multiple cargos in both Arabidopsis roots and hypocotyls.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: Plant cells utilize actin filaments for subcellular organelle trafficking, in contrast to mammalian cells which typically utilize microtubules.
source: In contrast to mammalian cells, which typically utilize microtubules for subcellular organelle trafficking, plant cells utilize actin filaments (Breuer et al., 2017; Geldner et al., 2001; Granger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Each plant cell has several Golgi apparatus (GA) fused with EE/TGN compartments, which is specific to plant systems.
source: Each cell has several Golgi apparatus (GA) fused with EE/TGN compartments; which is specific to plant systems (Kang et al., 2011; Viotti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The EE/TGN compartments continuously form at, mature and detach from the trans-side of the GA.
source: The EE/TGN compartments continuously form at, mature and detach from the trans-side of the GA (Kang et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EE/TGN compartments dynamically move along actin filaments.
source: and dynamically move along actin filaments (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is based on live imaging observations.

claim: Following depolymerizing or stabilizing the actin filaments, a complete halt in the dynamics of the GA and the EE/TGN was observed.
source: Following depolymerizing or stabilizing the actin filaments, we observed a complete halt in the dynamics of the GA and the EE/TGN, which resulted in local aggregations of EE/TGNs, as shown by imaging epidermal cells in hypocotyl (Figure 4A; Figure 4B and Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: This is based on imaging after drug treatments.

claim: Despite loss of dynamics and resulting aggregations, FM4-64 was still able to reach the agglomerated EE/TGN.
source: Despite this loss of dynamics, and the resulting aggregations also in root epidermal cells, we observed that FM4-64 was still able to reach the agglomerated EE/TGN (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy imaging after drug treatment.

claim: Pronounced defects in the post-endocytic trafficking of PIN2 were observed after prolonged actin perturbation.
source: Nonetheless, we observed pronounced defects in the post-endocytic trafficking of cargoes such as PIN2. PIN2-GFP, which is normally observed at late endosomes marked by ARA7, was strongly mislocalized after prolonged actin perturbation. This was manifested by abnormally high amount of PIN2 in the aggregated late endosomal structures in root cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy imaging after drug treatment.

claim: Interference of actin affected the arrival of PIN2 to the vacuole.
source: These trafficking defects are in agreement with our previous observation where interference of actin affected the arrival of PIN2 to the vacuole (Kleine-Vehn et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Actin is required for the GA and EE/TGN dynamics and for the overall efficiency of post-endocytic trafficking processes.
source: This suggests that actin is required for the GA and EE/TGN dynamics and for the overall efficiency of post-endocytic trafficking processes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of actin perturbation.

claim: A spatial and temporal correlation was observed between the appearance of a small branch of an actin subsidiary filament and the disappearance of CCVs from the PM.
source: We observed a spatial and temporal correlation between the appearance of a small branch of an actin subsidiary filament and the disappearance of CCVs from the PM (Video 1).
evidence: This is based on dual-channel TIRF-M imaging.

claim: CCVs, after scission and release, get whipped away by actin subsidiary filaments to move along the network of actin.
source: This could possibly mean that the CCVs, after the scission and release, get whipped away by actin subsidiary filaments to get them moving along the network of actin.
evidence: This is speculation based on observed spatial-temporal correlations.

claim: Fully formed CCVs were observed attached along actin filament in close proximity to intracellular endosomal membrane structures.
source: This live dynamic interaction is further supported by evidence from replicas of protoplasts where fully formed CCVs were observed attached along actin filament in close proximity to intracellular endosomal membrane structures (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on SEM observations.

claim: On their way below the PM, EE/TGN pick up/collect the scissioned CCVs.
source: While studying movement of these structures, we observed that on their way below the PM, they pick up/collect the scissioned CCVs (Figure 5A, Figure 5—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on TIRF-M imaging observations.

claim: There was a significant increase in the percentage of CCV tracks ending in the 'endosomal' ROIs compared to 'control' ROIs.
source: We found that there was a significant increase in the percentage of CCV tracks ending in the 'endosomal' ROIs compared to 'control' ROIs (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is based on automated endosomal pick-up analysis.

claim: Actin-organized movement of EEs aids collecting the CCVs after their scission.
source: providing unbiased and quantitative evidence that actin-organized movement of EEs aids collecting the CCVs after their scission.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the endosomal pick-up analysis.

claim: Many well established models of CME assume that CCVs shed their coat rapidly after the scission event.
source: Many well established models of CME assume that CCVs shed their coat rapidly after the scission event, in order to be able to fuse with EE (Beck et al., 1992; Böcking et al., 2011; Massol et al., 2006; Sekiya-Kawasaki et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The key mammalian uncoating proteins, auxilins and HSC70 proteins, have been shown to be crucial for efficient endocytosis.
source: The key mammalian uncoating proteins, auxilins and Heat shock cognate 71 kDa protein (HSC70) proteins, have been shown to be crucial for efficient endocytosis (Bai et al., 2010; Greener et al., 2000; Hirst et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2008; Yim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Auxilins appear to be conserved in plants but are not essential for endocytosis or development.
source: While auxilins appear to be conserved in plants, they are not essential for endocytosis or development (Adamowski et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Uncoating in plants may work differently than in mammalian systems.
source: implying that uncoating in plants may work differently.
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-essential nature of auxilins in plants.

claim: While some CCVs lose their clathrin coat, many others retained their coat all the way till they reached the EE/TGN compartment.
source: While closely following the CCVs and the EEs with TIRF-M in hypocotyl epidermis, we noticed that while some CCVs lose their clathrin coat (Video 2), many others retained their coat all the way till they reached the EE/TGN compartment (Figure 5A, Figure 5—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on TIRF-M imaging observations.

claim: The clathrin coat does not get disassembled immediately after scission, unlike in animal cells.
source: This implies that the clathrin coat does not get disassembled immediately after scission, unlike in animal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of coat retention.

claim: For CCVs immediately fusing with EEs, both clathrin coat and adaptor were retained until the vesicles reached the EE.
source: For the CCVs immediately fusing with EEs, both clathrin coat and adaptor were retained until the vesicles reached the EE.
evidence: This is based on dual-channel TIRF-M imaging observations.

claim: After fusion with EE, the EE compartment did not contain any visible adaptor, implying that the uncoating process had taken place immediately before or during the fusion.
source: However, after fusion, the EE compartment did not contain any visible adaptor, implying that the uncoating process had taken place, at least partially, but immediately before or during the fusion (Figure 6B and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on imaging observations.

claim: Aggregates of partially coated CCVs fused to the intracellular endosomal membrane were detected by ultrastructural analysis.
source: This hypothesis is supported also by ultrastructural analysis, where aggregates of partially coated CCVs fused to the intracellular endosomal membrane were detected (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is based on SEM observations.

claim: Some CCVs remain partially uncoated at the EE.
source: This also supports that some CCVs remain partially uncoated at the EE.
evidence: This is an inference based on ultrastructural observations.

claim: For CCVs being trafficked for a longer duration in the cytosol before reaching the EE, the loss of adaptor before clathrin coat was often observed.
source: For the CCVs being trafficked for a longer duration in the cytosol before reaching the EE, we were often able to observe the loss of adaptor before clathrin coat (Figure 6A and Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: This is based on dual-channel TIRF-M imaging observations.

claim: The disassembly of the released CCVs does not typically happen all at once but sequentially.
source: This means that the disassembly of the released CCVs does not typically happen all at once but sequentially.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of sequential loss of coat components.

claim: Sequential loss of coat was observed in the majority of cases (18/20 CCVs).
source: The sequential loss of coat was observed in the majority of cases (18/20 CCVs); whereas in the remaining traced CCVs both components vanished together.
evidence: This is based on quantification of dual-channel imaging observations.

claim: Partially uncoated CCVs can be detected deeper in the cytosol by TEM.
source: This sequential uncoating is also supported by TEM observations, in which we can detect partially uncoated CCVs deeper in the cytosol (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on TEM observations.

claim: In plants uncoating of the CCVs does not happen immediately after scission at the endocytic spot.
source: In summary, multiple independent observations show that in plants uncoating of the CCVs does not happen immediately (co-operative process) after scission at the endocytic spot, but the clathrin coat is retained for a prolonged time, shedding its components gradually (sequential process) on its way to the EE (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple observations.

claim: The clathrin coat is retained for a prolonged time, shedding its components gradually on its way to the EE.
source: In summary, multiple independent observations show that in plants uncoating of the CCVs does not happen immediately (co-operative process) after scission at the endocytic spot, but the clathrin coat is retained for a prolonged time, shedding its components gradually (sequential process) on its way to the EE (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple observations.

claim: The typical Arabidopsis CCVs possess a hexagonal clathrin basket coat, with an average diameter of 60 nm.
source: We determined that the typical Arabidopsis CCVs possess a hexagonal clathrin basket coat, with an average diameter of 60 nm.
evidence: This is based on ultrastructural analysis.

claim: Arabidopsis CCVs are located on the PM, on actin filaments and at aggregations at the EEs/TGNs.
source: They are located on the PM, on actin filaments and at aggregations at the EEs/TGNs.
evidence: This is based on ultrastructural analysis.

claim: The presence of small flat lattices suggests the existence of more than one mechanism of membrane bending within the plant system.
source: Moreover, the presence of small flat lattices, which could give rise to CCVs following 'constant area model' or recently described 'intermediate model' (Bucher et al., 2018; Scott et al., 2018), suggests the existence of more than one mechanism of membrane bending within the plant system.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations of flat lattices.

claim: The bona fide CME population had a mean lifetime of 42 s and accounted for 44% of the total CME events at the PM.
source: While the majority of the events were in fact transient and likely non-functional, the bona fide CME population had a mean lifetime of 42 s and accounted for 44% of the total CME events at the PM.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of TIRF-M data.

claim: The discovery of differences in the bona fide lifetime between tissues suggest that there are organ- and tissue-specific modulations of CME in plants.
source: The discovery of differences in the bona fide lifetime between tissues suggest that there are organ- and tissue-specific modulations of CME in plants.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed differences between root and hypocotyl.

claim: Compared to yeast models, the plant CME appears to be much faster and the resulting endocytic vesicles are almost twice the size.
source: Compared to yeast models (Lu et al., 2016), the plant CME appears to be much faster (considering all phases of CCV formation: assembly, maturation and scission) and the resulting endocytic vesicles are almost twice the size (Kaksonen and Roux, 2018).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous literature.

claim: Plants have differential regulatory processing of recycling clathrin compared to animals and yeast.
source: This suggests that plants have differential regulatory processing of recycling clathrin compared to animals and yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on differences in CME kinetics and vesicle sizes.

claim: CLC2 has a non-perfect localisation with CHC1.
source: It is important to note that our live imaging used CLC2 as a marker for CME, despite biochemical and genetic evidence that the CLCs interact with both CHC1 and CHC2 (Adamowski et al., 2018; Gadeyne et al., 2014) and the CHCs being genetically redundant for each other (Kitakura et al., 2011), we found a non-perfect localisation of CLC2 and CHC1.
evidence: This is based on co-localization analysis.

claim: Plants do not possess type one myosin.
source: Furthermore, plants do not possess type one myosin (the class of myosin involved in yeast endocytosis)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Actin or its associated proteins do not accumulate at the CME loci in plants.
source: and, more importantly, actin or its associated proteins do not accumulate at the CME loci.
evidence: This is based on imaging observations.

claim: In plants it is possible that clathrin polymerization energy, in addition to other membrane deforming proteins, might provide enough force to overcome the turgor pressure.
source: In this model, the curvature could be generated by the continuous polymerization of clathrin (Bucher et al., 2018; Scott et al., 2018), therefore in plants it is possible that clathrin polymerization energy, in addition to other membrane deforming proteins, might provide enough force to overcome the turgor pressure.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of membrane bending.

claim: Plant-specific mechanism of membrane bending must overcome turgor pressures higher than found in yeast, while producing larger CCVs (60 nm compared to 36 nm in Saccharomyces cerevisiae) and in a more rapid manner (33–42 s compared to 75–135 s).
source: It is noteworthy that plant-specific mechanism of membrane bending must overcome turgor pressures higher than found in yeast, while producing larger CCVs (60 nm compared to 36 nm in Saccharomyces cerevisiae Smaczynska-de Rooij et al., 2010) and in a more rapid manner (33–42 s compared to 75–135 s Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous literature.

claim: During the independent evolution of multi-cellularity in plants and animals, alternate membrane deformation mechanisms co-evolved in accordance to the differences in cell-cell adhesion, signalling and polarity between the model systems.
source: It is possible that during the independent evolution of multi-cellularity in plants and animals, alternate membrane deformation mechanisms co-evolved in accordance to the differences in cell-cell adhesion, signalling and polarity between the model systems (Eaton and Martin-Belmonte, 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: During actin disruption, endocytosed membrane still reached the aggregated EE/TGN structures.
source: However, during actin disruption, endocytosed membrane still reached the aggregated EE/TGN structures.
evidence: This is based on imaging observations after drug treatment.

claim: A passive Brownian motion of the freed CCVs is sufficient for the eventual reaching of CCVs the EEs.
source: This suggests that a passive Brownian motion of the freed CCVs is sufficient for the eventual reaching of CCVs the EEs.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations after actin disruption.

claim: Direct examination of protein cargos and their mis-localization following actin disruption suggested that actin-mediated EE mobility is a key requirement for a specific cargo sorting.
source: However, direct examination of protein cargos and their mis-localization following actin disruption suggested that actin-mediated EE mobility is a key requirement for a specific cargo sorting.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of cargo mislocalization.

claim: There is a strong spatio-temporal relationship between the actin filaments dynamic at the vicinity of the PM and CME events.
source: In support of this, we observed a strong spatio-temporal relationship between the actin filaments dynamic at the vicinity of the PM and CME events (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on imaging observations.

claim: There is a significant correlation between the termination of CME events at the PM and the targeted movement of the EE/TGN passing below.
source: Further to this, we also observed a significant correlation between the termination of CME events at the PM and the targeted movement of the EE/TGN passing below (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of endosomal pick-up.

claim: Fine actin filament dynamics and directional, actin-mediated TGN/EE movement have an active role in mediating CME events at the PM and organizing early post-endocytic trafficking.
source: This suggests a so far unappreciated active role of fine actin filament dynamics as well as the directional, actin-mediated TGN/EE movement in mediating CME events at the PM and organizing early post-endocytic trafficking.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations.

claim: In both yeast and animal cellular systems endocytic vesicles uncoat rapidly after the scission event with the aid of auxillin and HSC70 proteins.
source: In both yeast and animal cellular systems endocytic vesicles uncoat rapidly after the scission event with the aid of auxillin and HSC70 proteins (Böcking et al., 2011; Krantz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is some debate as to whether uncoating is an all-or-nothing process.
source: However, there is some debate as to whether uncoating is an all-or-nothing process (Schroeter et al., 2016; Trahey and Hay, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The uncoating process in plants has not been studied in any detail.
source: The uncoating process in plants has not been studied in any detail
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Deletion of auxillin-like proteins does not produce as strong effects on CME in plants as observed in mammalian systems.
source: while there are auxillin-like proteins, their deletion does not produce as strong effects on CME as observed in mammalian systems (Adamowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Plants may have different mechanisms to uncoat the CCVs or uncoating is less crucial than assumed.
source: This raises a possibility that plants have different mechanisms to uncoat the CCVs or uncoating is less crucial than assumed.
evidence: This is speculation based on the non-essential nature of auxilins.

claim: Retaining the clathrin coat till the CCVs fusion with the early endosomes is unheard of in other systems.
source: But retaining the clathrin coat till the CCVs fusion with the early endosomes is unheard of in other systems.
evidence: This is stated as a unique feature of plant CME.

claim: Sequential and severely delayed uncoating or even no loss of clathrin coat on the way of endocytic vesicles to the early endosomes is in stark contrast with current models of CME.
source: In summary, these observations revealed sequential and severely delayed uncoating or even no loss of clathrin coat on the way of endocytic vesicles to the early endosomes, which is in stark contrast with current models of CME.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion emphasizing the uniqueness of plant CME.

claim: Plant CME occurs much faster and generates much larger vesicles than yeast systems.
source: Plant CME appears to follow the constant curvature model of CCV formation occurring much faster and generating much larger vesicles than yeast systems (Kaksonen and Roux, 2018), of predominantly a hexagonal basket type.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous literature.

claim: Plants have evolved a unique mechanism of membrane bending against turgor.
source: Contrary to current paradigm, plant CME does not require actin suggesting that plants have evolved a unique mechanism of membrane bending against turgor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the actin-independence of plant CME.

claim: Actin is important in post-endocytoic events for movement of EEs and proper sorting of cargos.
source: Actin, nonetheless, is important in post-endocytoic events for movement of EEs and proper sorting of cargos.
evidence: This is based on observations of effects of actin perturbation on post-endocytic events.

claim: The presence of dynamic fine actin filaments and passing of mobile EE below the PM has a significant correlation with an increased rate of CME.
source: Importantly, the presence of dynamic fine actin filaments and passing of mobile EE below the PM has a significant correlation with an increased rate of CME
evidence: This is based on the endosomal pick-up analysis.

claim: Actin-mediated endosome movement has an unsuspected role in mediating CME at the PM and 'collecting' the post-endocytic vesicles.
source: thus highlighting an unsuspected role of actin-mediated endosome movement in mediating CME at the PM and 'collecting' the post-endocytic vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple observations.

claim: The strongly delayed uncoating and sequential removal of coat components is a unique feature of plant CME.
source: The strongly delayed uncoating and sequential removal of coat components is another unique feature of plant CME.
evidence: This is based on imaging observations of uncoating.

claim: Observations in complex, multi-cellular organs provide unprecedented insight into higher order interactions, which are otherwise absent in unicellular models.
source: These observations in complex, multi-cellular organs also provide unprecedented insight into higher order interactions, which are otherwise absent in unicellular models.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the experimental system used.

claim: Despite the presence of evolutionary conserved components, plant CME is mechanistically unique, presumably reflecting an independent evolution of multicellularity in plants versus other models.
source: Altogether, this study shows that despite the presence of evolutionary conserved components, plant CME is mechanistically unique, presumably reflecting an independent evolution of multicellularity in plants versus other models.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
